title: Vayelech: Moses went (Deuteronomy 31:1)
hook: at the end, Moses goes out to the people rather than calling them in
tomorrow: Vayelech: strong and of good courage (Deuteronomy 31:7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great choice: life and death, the blessing and the curse. Your line was choose life. Which fork did you take? Today, a new portion, a short one, and its first two words. Day five hundred twenty-two.

When an important person wants to speak with you, you usually go to them. You're called into the office. You wait outside a door. You're given a time slot. Leaders summon; that's part of what power looks like. At the very end of his life, Moses leads the whole camp. He could have every tribe brought before his tent. Nobody would have blamed him for it. And the portion opens with him doing the opposite.
screen: `CALLED INTO THE OFFICE.` → `LEADERS SUMMON.` → `MOSES DOES THE OPPOSITE.`

segments.voice: "And Moses went and spoke these words unto all Israel." In Hebrew, vayelech Moshe: and Moses went. Readers ask: went where? He wasn't on a journey. The text doesn't say. So the commentators fill the silence, each a little differently. Ibn Ezra suggests he went from tribe to tribe through the whole camp, to tell each one in person that he was about to die, and to strengthen them. Nachmanides pictures him going out to the people the way someone about to leave goes to say goodbye to a friend, as a mark of respect. Either way, the man who spoke with God doesn't call the people in for one final address. He walks to them. In the very next verse he tells them why he's saying goodbye: "I am a hundred and twenty years old this day; I can no more go out and come in." He says he can no longer go out and come in. And still, he goes out to them one more time. The portion named for this moment, Vayelech, is short: one chapter, thirty verses. Maybe that fits. A last visit doesn't need to be long. It needs to happen. A leaving can be done by announcement, by a notice on the wall. Moses chooses to do it in person, tent by tent.
screen: `VAYELECH: AND HE WENT.` · `WHERE? THE TEXT IS SILENT.` · `TRIBE BY TRIBE, TO SAY GOODBYE.` · `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY, STILL GOING.` · then, large: `HE WENT TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go to someone yourself. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you've been waiting to hear from. A friend who's gone quiet, a relative you only see when they visit you, a neighbor you'd talk to if only they knocked. Notice the waiting. Now picture reversing it. You walk to their door, or pick up the phone, or send the first message. Not a summons; a visit. See their face when it's you who came. The bell holds the time.
Vayelech. And he went. The first word of a short portion, one chapter long.
Your line: he went to them. Today, instead of waiting for someone to come to you, go to them: a visit, a call, a first message. Day five hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Vayelech is read in the fall, near Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and is often paired with Nitzavim; teachers draw from its opening the value of a leader going out to the people.

fork.reveal: and Moses went: the leader of the whole camp walks to the people to say goodbye.

original.note: Hebrew: and he went. the first word of Deuteronomy 31 and the name of the portion.

what it means: at the end, Moses goes out to the people instead of calling them in.
what a scholar hears: the verse never says where he went; Ibn Ezra says to each tribe, Nachmanides says to take leave like a friend.

notes: Deuteronomy 31:1–2 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory ('spoke' vs KJV 'spake'); verify.

Ibn Ezra on 31:1: he went to each tribe to tell them he would die and encourage them; Ramban: he went from the Levite camp to the people to take leave, as one leaving a friend. Paraphrased; verify attributions.
Vayelech as shortest parashah (30 verses): standard by verse count.
